title: Acceleration in different forms

match.reason: The bank point only teaches acceleration as dv/dt and integration back to velocity and displacement, and does not teach the v dv/dx or d/dx(½v²) forms, which is the new point's idea, so it is a different idea rather than a match.

draft.title: Acceleration in different forms
card: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. When velocity is given in terms of time t, use a = dv/dt.
When velocity is given in terms of position x, use a = v dv/dx. This comes from the chain rule: dv/dt = dv/dx × dx/dt, and dx/dt = v.
The same thing can be written a = d/dx(½v²). Differentiate ½v² with respect to x and you get v dv/dx.
Example: v² = 16 − x². Then ½v² = 8 − ½x², so a = d/dx(8 − ½x²) = −x.
draft.remember: Use dv/dt when v depends on t. Use v dv/dx or d/dx(½v²) when v depends on x.

a.q: A particle has velocity v = 3x at position x. Which expression gives its acceleration in terms of x?
a.why: With v = 3x, dv/dx = 3, so a = v dv/dx = 3x × 3 = 9x. The option dv/dx = 3 is only the rate of change of velocity with position, not with time.
a.clue: Velocity depends on x, so multiply dv/dx by v.

b.q: A particle moves so that v² = 25 − 4x². What is its acceleration at position x?
b.why: ½v² = 12.5 − 2x², so a = d/dx(12.5 − 2x²) = −4x. The option −8x comes from differentiating v² and forgetting the ½.
b.clue: Halve v² first, then differentiate with respect to x.

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is the longest and the only one that shows working (3x × 3), so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.
The clue 'multiply dv/dx by v' names the expression v dv/dx, which appears only in the right option, so it gives the answer away.

final.title: Acceleration in different forms
card: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. When velocity is given in terms of time \(t\), use \(a = \frac{dv}{dt}\).
When velocity is given in terms of position \(x\), use \(a = v\frac{dv}{dx}\). This comes from the chain rule: \(\frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{dv}{dx} \times \frac{dx}{dt}\), and \(\frac{dx}{dt} = v\).
The same thing can be written \(a = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{1}{2}v^{2}\right)\). Differentiate \(\frac{1}{2}v^{2}\) with respect to \(x\) and you get \(v\frac{dv}{dx}\).
final.remember: Use \(\frac{dv}{dt}\) when \(v\) depends on \(t\). Use \(v\frac{dv}{dx}\) or \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{1}{2}v^{2}\right)\) when \(v\) depends on \(x\).

a.q: A particle has velocity \(v = 3x\) at position \(x\). Which gives its acceleration in terms of \(x\)?
a.why: With \(v = 3x\), \(\frac{dv}{dx} = 3\), so \(a = v\frac{dv}{dx} = 3x \times 3 = 9x\). The option \(\frac{dv}{dx} = 3\) is the rate of change of velocity with position, not with time, so it is missing the factor \(v\).
a.clue: Velocity here depends on position. Which form suits that?

b.q: A particle moves so that \(v^{2} = 25 - 4x^{2}\). What is its acceleration at position \(x\)?
b.why: \(\frac{1}{2}v^{2} = 12.5 - 2x^{2}\), so \(a = \frac{d}{dx}\left(12.5 - 2x^{2}\right) = -4x\). The option \(-8x\) comes from differentiating \(v^{2}\) and forgetting the \(\frac{1}{2}\).
b.clue: Halve \(v^{2}\) first, then differentiate with respect to \(x\).
